references.title: Past Incident - Cloud Admin Session Hijack
references.content:
A cloud administrator account showed a successful login from an unfamiliar country after three MFA denials.
Within eight minutes the actor enumerated storage buckets, created a temporary access key, and added a mailbox
forwarding rule. The incident was confirmed after device logs showed no matching endpoint activity from the
administrator's managed laptop.

Lessons learned: prioritize token revocation over password reset alone, inspect OAuth grants, and verify whether
the session came from a managed device before assuming user travel.

Cloud infrastructure incidents should be correlated against cloud provider health, autoscaling activity, quota
limits, load balancer target health, DNS changes, IAM permission updates, network ACLs, and managed database events.

Immediate response focuses on restoring capacity or routing, avoiding destructive changes before evidence is
captured, and confirming whether the blast radius is zonal, regional, account-specific, or service-specific.

references.title: IT Operations Incident Runbook
references.content:
IT operations incidents should confirm impacted users, affected access path, device posture, identity provider
status, VPN concentrator health, email service status, DNS resolution, and network reachability.

Response should include scope confirmation, workaround guidance, service-owner escalation, and a user-facing
communication update when many users are affected.

references.title: Production Incident Triage Runbook
references.content:
Production incident triage starts with impact scope, recent changes, service health, and mitigation options.

High priority signals include customer-facing 5xx errors, elevated latency, failed dependencies, saturation,
database connection exhaustion, queue backlog, and a recent deploy or configuration change.

Recommended actions include checking deployment history, reviewing dashboards, comparing upstream and downstream
error rates, rolling back risky changes, scaling saturated components, and communicating impact and mitigation status.

references.title: Past Incident - Cloud Admin Session Hijack
references.content:
A cloud administrator account showed a successful login from an unfamiliar country after three MFA denials.
Within eight minutes the actor enumerated storage buckets, created a temporary access key, and added a mailbox
forwarding rule. The incident was confirmed after device logs showed no matching endpoint activity from the
administrator's managed laptop.

Lessons learned: prioritize token revocation over password reset alone, inspect OAuth grants, and verify whether
the session came from a managed device before assuming user travel.

Treat a login anomaly as high risk when two or more signals are present:

- Impossible travel or a new country for the user.
- MFA fatigue, repeated push denials, or a push accepted after many failures.

disabling suspicious OAuth grants, and preserving identity provider logs.

Recommended remediation for likely identity compromise:

1. Revoke active sessions and refresh tokens.
2. Reset the account password and require MFA reset from a trusted device.
3. Remove suspicious OAuth app grants and mailbox forwarding rules.
4. Block or challenge the source IP and related infrastructure.
5. Review privileged actions, data access, and lateral movement for the next 24 hours.
6. Open a user verification task with the service desk.

references.title: Account Takeover Triage Playbook
references.content:
Treat a login anomaly as high risk when two or more signals are present:

- Impossible travel or a new country for the user.
- MFA fatigue, repeated push denials, or a push accepted after many failures.
- Login from a new ASN, proxy, VPN, hosting provider, or Tor exit node.
- Successful login followed by mailbox rule creation, OAuth consent, privilege changes, or data export.
- Failed logins against multiple users from the same IP address.

Immediate containment includes revoking refresh tokens, resetting credentials, requiring MFA re-registration,
disabling suspicious OAuth grants, and preserving identity provider logs.

# VPN Troubleshooting Knowledge Base

## Overview
This article explains how to troubleshoot VPN connectivity issues for enterprise users.

## Common Symptoms
Users may report that the VPN disconnects frequently, fails after a password reset, shows an authentication error, or cannot connect to the company network.

## Troubleshooting Steps
1. Confirm the user can log in to the Single Sign-On portal.
2. Ask the user to restart the VPN client.
3. Verify that Duo MFA approval is working.
4. Clear saved VPN credentials from the VPN client.
5. Confirm the user is using the latest VPN client version.
6. Ask the user to reconnect using the new password if the password was recently changed.

## Escalation
If the issue continues after these steps, route the ticket to Network Support.

## Ticket Category
VPN Connectivity

## Assigned Team
Network Support

## Default Priority
Medium

# Duo MFA Knowledge Base

## Overview
This article explains how to troubleshoot Duo Multi-Factor Authentication issues.

## Common Symptoms
Users may report that they are not receiving Duo push notifications, cannot approve MFA, changed phones, or lost access to their authentication device.

## Troubleshooting Steps
1. Verify that the user has network connectivity on their mobile device.
2. Ask the user to open the Duo Mobile app manually.
3. Ask the user to check whether push notifications are enabled.
4. If the user changed phones, re-register the new device.
5. If the user lost the device, verify identity and issue a temporary bypass code according to policy.

## Escalation
If the user cannot complete MFA after basic troubleshooting, route the ticket to Identity and Access Management.

## Ticket Category
Multi-Factor Authentication

## Assigned Team
Identity and Access Management

## Default Priority
Medium

Treat a login anomaly as high risk when two or more signals are present:

- MFA fatigue, repeated push denials, or a push accepted after many failures.

disabling suspicious OAuth grants, and preserving identity provider logs.

Recommended remediation for likely identity compromise:

1. Revoke active sessions and refresh tokens.
2. Reset the account password and require MFA reset from a trusted device.
3. Remove suspicious OAuth app grants and mailbox forwarding rules.
4. Block or challenge the source IP and related infrastructure.
5. Review privileged actions, data access, and lateral movement for the next 24 hours.
6. Open a user verification task with the service desk.

references.content:

- Check whether the same user created inbox rules, changed MFA methods, consented to OAuth apps, or downloaded data.
- Compare the user agent and device ID to the user's normal login history.

# Password Reset Knowledge Base

## Overview
This article explains how users can reset their enterprise account password and regain access to systems connected through Single Sign-On.

## Common Symptoms
Users may report that they forgot their password, their account is locked, or they cannot log in after changing their password.

## Troubleshooting Steps
1. Ask the user to visit the enterprise Single Sign-On password reset portal.
2. Verify the user's identity using the approved recovery method.
3. Reset the password and wait 5 to 10 minutes for synchronization.
4. Ask the user to sign out of all active sessions.
5. Ask the user to log in again using the new password.
6. If the account is locked, wait for the lockout period or escalate to Identity and Access Management.

## Escalation
If the user cannot reset the password or the account remains locked, route the ticket to Identity and Access Management.

## Ticket Category
Account Access

## Assigned Team
Identity and Access Management

## Default Priority
Medium

# Password Reset Knowledge Base

## Overview
This article explains how users can reset their enterprise account password and regain access to systems connected through Single Sign-On.

## Common Symptoms
Users may report that they forgot their password, their account is locked, or they cannot log in after changing their password.

## Troubleshooting Steps
1. Ask the user to visit the enterprise Single Sign-On password reset portal.
2. Verify the user's identity using the approved recovery method.
3. Reset the password and wait 5 to 10 minutes for synchronization.
4. Ask the user to sign out of all active sessions.
5. Ask the user to log in again using the new password.
6. If the account is locked, wait for the lockout period or escalate to Identity and Access Management.

## Escalation
If the user cannot reset the password or the account remains locked, route the ticket to Identity and Access Management.

## Ticket Category
Account Access

## Assigned Team
Identity and Access Management

## Default Priority
Medium
